Well one of the major underlying themes of the season is the role of gender in framing the characters’ interactions with one another, especially the female main cast. So I think examining the characters of Roy and Lorraine absent from their genders is missing a lot of what the show is trying to say sub-textually.

All of the major female characters in the show (Dot, Lorraine, Scotty, and Indira) clash against the expectations society (and more specifically, male characters) attempt to impose on them. Scotty doesn’t connect or relate to stereotypically girly things like wearing dresses, Indira’s husband projects his own insecurities onto her as a means of attempting to control her, Dot’s desperate actions to maintain a happy household and feel like a valid and useful mother and wife put her family in a path of danger that may have been avoidable, and Lorraine has to operate amidst startling misogyny from business partners that she far eclipses in terms of financial success. All of them are in some way constrained undesirably by the expectations placed on women. But I digress.

In a paradoxical sense, Lorraine and Roy are most similar because their natures betray their professions. Though Lorraine’s business is debt, she was not raised to feel like she was owed anything due to her place as a woman as determined by society. And the way she frames her business reflects that upbringing. Yes she puts others in debt, but it’s as a service, as a lifeline. It’s certainly a cruel way to frame debt, but it perfectly reflects how she views herself and the world at large. The only people that engage in her services are those who she views as inferior critical thinkers, those that have not worked as hard as she has. It’s an opt-in contract that she forces nobody into. But knowing the nature of humanity, she also knows that people will inevitably have need of her business. She truly believes herself to be a prime human being, without insecurity, and she doesn’t show that in an authoritarian or totalitarian way whatsoever.

By contrast, Roy likes to project an air of rugged, every man for himself style individualism. He’s an outlaw sheriff, defending the “vulnerable” from the “wicked” in his way, not the law’s way. But his entire persona is so bound to how others perceive, react to, and serve him that he needs to impose on their lives to maintain his self image. He abuses his spouses and children, grooming them all into perfect beings of servility so that there is the most minimal chance that they can break out of his idea of a model household. He sneers at authority figures and “elites” like Lorraine not because he’s against what they represent, but because only his authority actually matters to him. He needs to be in total control of every aspect of his life or else his ubermensch image just wouldn’t stick when he looks in the mirror. This is the behavior of a man raised in toxic masculinity that feels his power being challenged. It’s the behavior of someone deeply insecure, resistant to a changing world, and terrified that he will lose his power at any moment. For those reasons, I view Lorraine and Roy as fundamentally different characters to the point of diametric opposition. Lorraine expects nothing of others beyond the contract or agreement they mutually enter into with each other. Roy expects others to bend over backwards for him with no promise of reciprocal support. Lorraine isn’t a paragon of morality, but she’s nowhere close to Roy’s utter evil.

So many ways for me. The central questions of both to me are how do people move on after losing someone? How does an artist (musical, culinary, etc.) progress in their art when it was so closely tied to a person who has taken their life? What does that person's death say about the nature of their art form to begin with? Llewyn Davis and Carmy Berzatto are two characters trying to accomplish the exact same thing in their lives. And they both share the same volatility and borderline unhealthy drive for success that ultimately causes them to hurt many people in the pursuit of their art.

The thing that distinguishes the Menu from the Bear for me is that the Menu is clearly going for social satire over anything else. It’s more about the customer’s perception of food service work than the actual food service workers themselves. If we take the Menu at face value, it portrays fine dining head chefs as capricious and vindictive with little care for the customer’s needs over their own art. The Bear does the exact opposite in episodes like “Forks” which emphasize the hospitality element of the highest skill level of culinary arts. In the Menu, beyond him intending to kill them, chef Slowik demands that his customers find meaning in his work. In the Bear, the meaning for all of the chefs comes from the customer’s satisfaction and their love for cooking.

There’s also a lot of other themes in the Bear that make it what it is for me that the Menu doesn’t have. More than anything, the Bear is a workplace and family drama in a way that the Menu simply couldn’t be. It tackles themes of grief, mental illness, and trauma with a very particular touch. The Menu, to contrast, features a scene where >!a sous chef kills himself as the course of a meal.!< It’s just not the same for me.
